caseno: Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 36 of 1997.
lawyer:
K S Nabi, Attorney-General (Serajul Huq, Senior Advocate with him), instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on Record ---- For the Petitioner.
Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ---- For the Respondent.
parties:
State ----- Petitioner
vs. 
Jobaida Rashid ----- Accused Respondent
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: State is seeking leave to appeal from judgment and order dated 23 March, 1997 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Criminal Misc. Case No. 552 of 1997 making the Rule absolute and granting bail to the accused respondent, Mrs. Jobaida Rashid, pending disposal of Sessions Case No. 319 of 1997 in the Court of the Sessions Judge, Dhaka. 

 2. The respondent is the wife of the absconding accused Lt. Col. Khondker Abdur Rashid. who along with the respondent and many others is facing trial in the aforesaid Sessions Case which arose out of Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10) 96 (GR Case No. 2923 of 1996). The case started on an FIR filed on 2-10-96 by AFM Mohitul Islam, receptionist-cum-resident PA at the Dhanmondi residence of the then President of Bangladesh, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahmanon the fateful night of 14 August, 1975 and related to the dreadful incident of that night in which the President and his family members and others were killed by some army officers and others as mentioned in the FIR. 

 3. The respondent in her petition before the High Court Division alleged, inter alia, that in connection with the aforesaid case Police made search in her Gulshan residence on 14-8-96 and 12-10-96 for finding out her husband who has been residing there. The Police forcibly entered into the house by creating an atmosphere of terror intimidation and panic. Similar forcible entry and search of the house had taken place also at night on 2nd November, 1996. There were altercation and exchange of hot words between the respondent and the Police Officers inducting officers of CID and on every occasion they threatened the respondent and said that they would teach her a lesson. The Police upon search produced one licensed pistol of the respondent from her bedroom and a revolver and shot gun were recovered earlier by them on 12-10-96 from the bedroom of her husband. The arms and ammunition were all licensed and there were no arms and ammunition which were illegally kept/stored or preserved by the respondent. A seizure list was prepared at the mid-night of 2-11-96 and the respondent was forced under threat, coercion and intimidation to sign the said disputed seizure list but she protested the preparation of the false seizure list. She cannot read or write Bengali. On this occasion also there was altercation between the respondent and the Police officers. The respondent later on learnt that the Police prepared an incorrect and concocted seizure list showing extra ammunition which they had either planted or brought inside the house beyond the knowledge of the respondent. The police officials during the second round of altercation became furious and said that although they had initially come for her husband in connection with the aforesaid case but now she would have to face music in connection with that case also and asked her to go to Gulshan Police Station along with them at that hour of night. On 3-11-96 she was taken to the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and brought on Police remand for 5 days and during that period she was unbearably, mentally and physically, tortured which may be described as uncivilised and brutal. She was shown to be an accused in Gulshan PS Case No. 9(11)96 dated 2-11-96 which was started in connection with recovery of arms and ammunition on 12-10-96 (which are all licensed). The respondent while on Police remand during 5 days between 3rd and 8th November, 1996 was inhumanly treated and deprived of essential medicare when she was badly sick during that period. 

 4. On 9-11-96 she was produced before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and the Court ordered her to be sent to the Jail Hajat. Instead of sending her to the Jail Hajat she was again brought on Police remand for 4 days showing her arrested in Sheikh Mujib murder case being Case No. 10(10)96 of Dhanmondi PS. During the second period of remand she was subjected to shocking, shameful and unbearable pressure and torture both mental and physical and intimidation. She was told that until and unless she agreed to sign a confessional statement in connection with the aforesaid Dhanmondi PS case there would be torture on her and also on her two unmarried daughters which would be intensified and prolonged. In such circumstance she was taken to the Magistrate on 12-11-96 who took her signature on a statement not made by her. The signature was given in the statement under duress, coercion, pressure, torture and inducement. The alleged confessional statement is liable to be retracted, cancelled and withdrawn. 

 5. On 28-11-96 the respondent who is an aged and sick woman and subjected to aforesaid barbaric treatment, prayed for bail in the Court of CMM, Dhaka which was refused. The prayer for bail having also been refused by the Additional Sessions Judge, Dhaka the respondent moved the High Court Division and obtained a Rule in the Misc. case. 

 7. The High Court Division after considering the materials on record against the respondent, namely, the FIR, charge-sheet, the alleged confessional statement and statements of three witnesses under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Maj. Gen. (Retd.) KM Shafiullah, AVM (Retd.) AK Khandker, Maj. Gen. (Retd.) M. Khalilur Rahman and also the submissions made by the parties held that the respondent had succeeded in making out a very good case for bail and that mere naming her in the charge-sheet without any prima facie material cannot be a good ground for refusal of bail. 

 8. The learned Attorney-General sought permission to allow Mr. Serajul Huq, who has been appointed a Special Public Prosecutor in the aforesaid case, to address us because of his special knowledge of the facts of the case. The learned Attorney-General submitted that he would make one or two submissions, if necessary, to supplement those of Mr. Serajul Huq. 

 9. Mr. Huq referred to the same materials, namely, charge-sheet, the statements under sections 164 and 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which were considered by the High Court Division, and submitted that there are materials on record from which it should appear that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the respondent has been guilty of an offence of criminal conspiracy which is punishable with death or imprisonment for life. Mr. Huq submitted that having regard to the said materials and the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court Division failed to exercise proper discretion in allowing the respondent to be enlarged on bail. 

 14. The learned Attorney-General in a bid to supplement the arguments of Mr. Huq, criticized the impugned judgment saying that it lacked proper adherence to the principles as are required to be followed in such matters and further a proper appreciation of the facts on record. The learned Attorney-General then submitted, as he did in the High Court Division, that this was a sensational case and on the date of occurrence the entire family of the then President of the country were done to death and the nation wanted that the real culprits should be punished. To this kind of argument, it will be enough to refer, which we did not want to out of deference, to what the High Court Division has said in reply and that is, "the mere fact that in the occurrence the head of the State with his family has been murdered and the mere fact this is a sensational case cannot be a ground for refusal of bail." We shall only add "to the respondent". 

 15. The only question is whether there are reasonable grounds as indicated above for refusing bail, to the respondent. The law permits granting of bail, even in a case where there are such reasonable grounds for refusing bail, in the case of any woman or any sick or infirm person. However, the respondent has not been granted bail upon these considerations but upon the view that there are no reasonable grounds for believing that she has been guilty of the offence alleged. The learned Attorney-General could not refer to any principle which has been allegedly violated by the High Court Division nor to any fact which has either been ignored or wrongly relied upon.
